104: ## Hard Rules — Non-Negotiable
105: 
106: 1. Never write implementation code during spec phase — markdown files only
107: 2. Never use `@CircuitBreaker` annotation in reactive pipelines — `CircuitBreakerOperator` only
108: 3. Never use `@Cacheable` inside a `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>` chain — `ReactiveRedisTemplate` + cache-aside
109: 4. Never block a Netty event loop thread — `BlockHound` catches it in tests
110: 5. Never put secrets in HCL, `application.yml` committed to Git, or `.env` files committed to Git
111: 6. Always name Resilience4J instances `fabt-{target}` (e.g., `fabt-hmis-bitfocus`)
112: 7. Always define cache names as constants in a `CacheNames` interface — never magic strings
113: 8. Always document the reactive boundary explicitly in `design.md`
114: 9. Always tag Terraform bootstrap tasks as `[BOOTSTRAP]` in `tasks.md`
115: 10. Do NOT use planning mode (Shift+Tab Shift+Tab) — it blocks file creation
116: 11. Never store or log any PII — queries describe needs, not persons
117: 12. DV shelter (`dv_shelter = true`) data access must be enforced at the DATA LAYER —
118:     routing-level checks are not sufficient and will not pass verify
119: 13. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on all concurrent availability snapshot inserts —
120:     read-before-write has a race condition under concurrent shelter updates
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## Domain-Specific Hard-Won Lessons
125: 
126: *(In addition to the 48 lessons in portfolio CLAUDE-CODE-BRIEF.md)*
127: 
128: **D1. Data age always surfaces to the caller.**
129: Every availability query response MUST include `data_age_seconds` derived from
130: `snapshot_ts`. A stale-cache hit that silently returns 3-hour-old data is worse
131: than returning nothing — the social worker drives across town to a shelter that
132: has been full since 9pm. Surface the staleness; never hide it.
133: 
134: **D2. `beds_available` is a derived field, not a stored field.**
135: Never store `beds_available` as a column. Derive it:
136: `beds_total - beds_occupied - beds_on_hold`. Storing it creates a consistency
137: hazard when concurrent reservations and updates overlap.
138: 
139: **D3. Availability updates are append-only snapshots.**
140: Never UPDATE a `BedAvailability` row. Insert a new snapshot and query the
141: latest by `snapshot_ts`. This gives you a complete audit trail and eliminates
142: update conflicts entirely. The CoC analytics pipeline reads the history.
143: 
144: **D4. The DV boundary is a data-layer rule, not a routing rule.**
145: Do not implement DV shelter privacy as an API gateway filter or a service-layer
146: `if (dv_shelter)` check. The boundary must be in the PostgreSQL Row Level
147: Security policy. A misconfigured route should return an empty result, not a
148: location. Verify with a test that directly queries the DB as a non-DV-role user.
149: 
150: **D5. Shelter coordinators update on mobile, standing up, under stress.**
151: The update UI must work in one hand on a phone with a cracked screen. Never
152: require a login per session — use a long-lived API key tied to the shelter.
153: Never require more than 3 taps to submit a routine bed count update. Test
154: the update flow with simulated 3G throttling in CI.
155: 
156: **D6. Cache invalidation must be synchronous with the write.**
157: When a coordinator submits an update, invalidate the L1 and L2 cache entries
158: for that shelter BEFORE returning 200 OK to the caller. Do not rely on TTL
159: expiry. A coordinator who refreshes their app and sees the old number will
160: stop trusting the system.

23: ### The Problem
24: 
25: A family of five is sitting in a parking lot at midnight. A social worker has 30 minutes before the family stops cooperating. Right now, that social worker is making phone calls — to shelters that may be closed, full, or unable to serve that family's specific needs. There is no shared system for real-time shelter bed availability in most US communities.
26: 
27: Commercial software does not serve this space because there is no profit motive. Homeless services operate on tight grants with no margin for per-seat licensing. The result: social workers keep personal spreadsheets, shelter coordinators answer midnight phone calls, and families wait in parking lots while the system fails them.
28: 
29: ### The Goal
30: 
31: An open-source platform that matches individuals and families experiencing homelessness to available shelter beds in real time. Designed to reduce total crisis-to-placement time from an estimated 55–140 minutes (serial phone calls, stale spreadsheets) to 25–45 minutes by providing real-time bed availability with a 3-tap hold to secure the bed during transport. Three deployment tiers (Lite, Standard, Full) ensure any community — from a rural volunteer-run CoC to a metro area with 50 shelters — can adopt the platform at a cost they can sustain.
32:

72: ## OpenSpec Workflow
73: 
74: ### What Is OpenSpec?
75: 
76: [OpenSpec](https://openspec.dev) is a lightweight spec-driven development framework designed for AI coding assistants. Specifications, proposals, and designs live in the repository alongside code — ensuring every feature is documented before it is implemented.
77: 
78: GitHub: [https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec)
79: 
80: ### How We Use It
81: 
82: Every feature starts as an OpenSpec change and follows this lifecycle:
83: 
84: 1. **Proposal** — Business case and scope
85: 2. **Design** — Architecture decisions and trade-offs
86: 3. **Specs** — Capability specifications with requirements and scenarios
87: 4. **Tasks** — Implementation task list with checkpoints
88: 5. **Implementation** — Code written against the spec
89: 6. **Verification** — `/opsx:verify` confirms implementation matches specs
90: 7. **Archive** — Change is finalized and archived
91:
